slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by presenting a Riemannian submersion as a controlled loss of dimension rather than as an arbitrary projection. The lecture follows the information that survives in the base, the information that lives in the fibers, and the correction terms that appear when those two directions fail to separate cleanly.

slides.label: Roadmap
slides.notes: This slide gives students the conceptual map before definitions arrive. The important phrase is interaction terms: without them a submersion would be little more than a product written with a projection. The chapter becomes powerful because those terms are explicit enough to use in curvature and Einstein equations.

slides.label: Submersion Definition
slides.notes: Emphasize that the definition is metric, not just differential-topological. A submersion gives many possible horizontal complements, but the Riemannian metric selects the orthogonal one. The base metric is exactly the metric that makes horizontal vectors project without changing length.

slides.label: Vertical Horizontal
slides.notes: This is a bookkeeping slide, but it is essential bookkeeping. Students should become comfortable decomposing a vector before asking about curvature. The tensors introduced next are built by differentiating these components and watching where the result lands.

slides.label: ONeill Tensors
slides.notes: The notation can look forbidding, so attach each tensor to a physical question. If horizontal directions are differentiated, do they remain horizontal? If fiber directions are differentiated, do they remain inside the fiber? The answers are precisely the correction terms that later enter curvature.

slides.label: Curvature Transfer
slides.notes: This is one of the lecture's anchor formulas. The sign and the factor are memorable because they say that the base curvature sees twisting of the horizontal distribution. Use it to warn students that projection is not curvature-neutral even when horizontal lengths are preserved.

slides.label: Sectional Planes
slides.notes: Pause here to classify every curvature formula by the plane it studies. Horizontal planes are easiest to remember because of the base comparison, but vertical and mixed planes are just as important for Ricci curvature. Ricci is a trace, so it necessarily sums information across all three channels.

slides.label: Ricci Trace
slides.notes: Connect this slide back to the course theme. Sectional curvature formulas are local measurements, but the Einstein condition asks for a tensor trace to be proportional to the metric. The lecture's calculations matter because they make that trace balance computable in structured families.

slides.label: Canonical Variation
slides.notes: Canonical variation is one of the chapter's most useful construction devices. It turns an infinite-dimensional metric question into a parameter search inside a geometrically meaningful family. The central teaching point is that scaling fibers changes curvature anisotropically, so an Einstein metric may occur at special parameter values.

slides.label: Hopf Prototype
slides.notes: This slide is deliberately schematic rather than a copied figure. The point is to provide a mental model for the chapter's examples: fibers can be genuine geometric circles, not just abstract kernels. Once the fiber direction is visible, canonical variation becomes a concrete operation.

slides.label: Homogeneous Applications
slides.notes: The chapter uses submersions as a bridge from group structure to curvature formulas. In a homogeneous quotient, the decomposition is not merely local; symmetry keeps the same algebraic pattern everywhere. This makes the Einstein equation much more approachable than it would be for an arbitrary metric.

slides.label: Warped Products
slides.notes: Warped products should be contrasted with canonical variation. In canonical variation the fiber scale is a constant parameter, while in a warped product the scale is a function on the base. That functional dependence brings gradient and Hessian terms into the Ricci equations.

slides.label: Einstein Recipe
slides.notes: This table turns the chapter into a reusable workflow. It also helps students avoid treating examples as isolated tricks. Each construction can be read as an answer to the same four questions: split, measure, trace, and tune.

slides.label: Pitfalls
slides.notes: Use this as a diagnostic slide during discussion. Each warning corresponds to a real source of wrong calculations: ignoring the metric condition, assuming a product when the horizontal distribution twists, or treating canonical variation like ordinary scaling. The cure in each case is to return to the splitting and compute the tensor terms.

slides.label: Learner Lab
slides.notes: These prompts are designed for short pauses rather than long problem sessions. The first checks the basic splitting, the second checks the meaning of the A tensor, and the third checks canonical variation. They also prepare students to read the chapter's examples as structured computations.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the chapter back to the course arc. Earlier chapters supplied homogeneous examples and Einstein equations; this chapter explains how fibered geometry transports curvature between spaces. The practical lesson is that many Einstein constructions become visible once vertical and horizontal directions are kept separate.
